# Incident Report: MTA-2026-01-31 PCAP Forensic Analysis

**Evidence analyzed:** `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 frames, 623.9 sec, 26.4 MB). No separate IDS/Suricata alert files were present in the evidence directory — findings below are derived solely from packet-level analysis via `tshark`.

## 1. Victim / Infected Host

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.1.21.58** | DHCP lease (frames 1–4) |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** (Intel NIC) | DHCP `eth.src`, confirmed by ARP announcements |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** | DHCP Option 12, NBNS name registrations |
| NetBIOS workgroup / AD domain | WIN11OFFICE / win11office.com | NBNS `<00>`/`<20>`/`<1e>` records, DNS SRV queries for `_ldap._tcp...win11office.com` |
| Logged-in Windows user | **gwyatt** | Kerberos exchanges (CNameString `gwyatt`) between 10.1.21.58 and domain controller 10.1.21.2 (WIN-LU4L24X3UB7) |

Note: LDAP/DRSUAPI/SAMR/LSARPC traffic between the host and the DC (10.1.21.2) consists of routine `DsCrackNames`/`DsBind` calls tied to normal domain logon — not DCSync or AD reconnaissance. This is background AD noise, not part of the attack.

## 2. Malware Family

**Attribution: behavioral only — NOT signature-confirmed.**

No executable was recovered in cleartext from the capture (the actual payload delivery occurred over TLS-encrypted sessions and its contents are unrecoverable without keys), and no known-malware string, hash, or YARA-class signature was observed. Based on observed behavior, this is a **browser-fingerprinting stealer/loader distributed via a fake file-download lure chain**, using a JS-based "fingerprint gate" that harvests full browser/system/canvas/WebRTC fingerprints and reports them to an HTTP(S) check-in panel (`whitepepper.su`) before further activity. The lure-domain naming pattern (`megafilehub`, `filemegahab`) and Cloudflare-fronted infrastructure with disposable TLDs (`.lat`, `.sbs`, `.cc`, `.cyou`) is consistent with commodity stealer distribution campaigns, but this is an assessment, not a confirmed family name.

## 3. Timeline (relative to capture start)

| t (s) | Event |
|---|---|
| 0.0 | DHCP assigns 10.1.21.58 to DESKTOP-ES9F3ML |
| 45.3 | TLS ClientHello SNI=`hiyter.com` (104.21.22.231) |
| 45.8 | TLS ClientHello SNI=`media.megafilehub4.lat` (104.21.48.156) — fake download lure |
| 48.3 | TLS ClientHello SNI=`arch.filemegahab4.sbs` (104.21.46.67) — second fake download lure |
| 90.3 | TLS ClientHello SNI=`whooptm.cyou` (62.72.32.156) |
| 92.3–96.6 | HTTP GET/POST to `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49:80) spoofing `agent=Chrome`; fingerprint payload served, then POSTed back |
| 103.0–104.0 | Repeat cycle spoofing `agent=Edge` |
| 109.2–121.8 | Ten rapid, near-identical-sized TLS sessions to 153.92.1.49:443 (beacon burst) plus one high-volume session (~1.5 MB) |
| 122.8 | TLS ClientHello SNI=`holiday-forever.cc` (80.97.160.24) |
| 126.5 | TLS ClientHello SNI=`communicationfirewall-security.cc` (104.21.9.36 / 172.67.141.109) |
| 623.9 | Capture ends |

## 4. Indicators of Compromise

### Command-and-control endpoints (IP:port)
- **153.92.1.49:80** — `whitepepper.su`, plaintext HTTP check-in/exfil panel (primary C2)
- **153.92.1.49:443** — `whitepepper.su`, TLS beaconing (repeated short sessions + one 1.5 MB session)
- **62.72.32.156:443** — `whooptm.cyou`
- **104.21.9.36:443** — `communicationfirewall-security.cc` (Cloudflare-fronted; origin possibly 172.67.141.109)
- **80.97.160.24:443** — `holiday-forever.cc`

### Malicious domains
- `whitepepper.su` → 153.92.1.49 (C2 panel)
- `whooptm.cyou` → 62.72.32.156
- `communicationfirewall-security.cc` → 104.21.9.36, 172.67.141.109
- `holiday-forever.cc` → 80.97.160.24
- `media.megafilehub4.lat` → 104.21.48.156, 172.67.154.67 (fake download lure)
- `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` → 104.21.46.67, 172.67.136.13 (fake download lure)
- `hiyter.com` → 104.21.22.231, 172.67.207.145 (first domain in the chain)

### Malicious URLs (fully recovered, plaintext)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log` (POST — exfiltrates system/browser/canvas/WebRTC fingerprint)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log` (POST)
- `http://whitepepper.su/favicon.ico`

Bot identifiers issued by the C2 panel: `id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C`, `token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b`

### Transferred file names / hashes
- The C2 (`whitepepper.su`) returned the plaintext response `cant open archive 172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bda042ad17a1.zip` to both the Chrome- and Edge-spoofed check-ins. This is a **filename reference from the C2**, not a file captured in the traffic:
  - `172.56.88.98` — appears to be the victim's external/NAT-egress IPv4 (a T-Mobile US carrier-grade NAT range), used by the panel to tag this victim's session.
  - `038485b1855ec7a1ba5bda042ad17a1` — a 32-hex-character identifier (**MD5-length, not SHA256**).
- **No SHA256 hash of any transferred file was observed anywhere in this capture.** The actual malware payload delivery (via TLS to `hiyter.com`, `media.megafilehub4.lat`, `arch.filemegahab4.sbs`) is fully encrypted and its file contents/hashes are not recoverable from this pcap without TLS key material.
